title: Closest Pair of Clock Times
statement:
You get a list of times on a 24-hour clock, each written as "HH:MM" (from "00:00" to "23:59"). The list may contain the same time more than once.

Return the smallest number of minutes between any two entries. The clock is a circle: you may measure the gap either way round, so midnight is not a wall. "23:58" and "00:03" are 5 minutes apart.

examples.why: 09:05 and 09:15 are 10 minutes apart. Every other pair is hours apart.
Measured across midnight, 23:50 to 00:20 is 30 minutes. Comparing only neighbors in sorted order, without the wrap, gives 690.
Exactly half a day apart, so both directions give 720.

constraints: Each time is a valid "HH:MM" string
hints: Turn each time into a single number: minutes since midnight. Now it is a question about numbers on a circle of length 1440.
After sorting, the closest pair must be next to each other in sorted order, except for one extra pair that goes around midnight.
Sort the minutes, take the smallest gap between neighbors, and also check first + 1440 − last. There are only 1440 possible values, so with more entries than that a duplicate is guaranteed.

explain.intuition:
Once every time is minutes since midnight, the times are points on a circle of length 1440. On a straight line, the closest pair of points is always a pair of neighbors after sorting: any pair further apart in sorted order has a neighbor pair between them that is at least as close.

A circle adds exactly one more neighbor pair: the last time of the day and the first time of the next day. Its gap is first + 1440 − last. Forgetting it is the classic bug, and it is like a timeline component that forgets an event at 23:55 is close to one at 00:05.
steps: If there are more than 1440 entries, two must be equal: return 0.
Sort the minutes (or mark them in a 1440-slot array, which sorts for free).
Take the smallest difference between neighbors, and compare it with the wrap gap first + 1440 − last.
pitfalls: Skipping the wrap pair across midnight, so ["23:50", "00:20"] gives 1410 instead of 30.
Comparing the strings instead of minutes. String order works for sorting here, but subtracting needs numbers.
Forgetting duplicates. Two equal times give 0, and the bucket version must notice a slot that is already marked.

complexity.time: O(n log n), or O(n + 1440) with buckets

solutions.title: Compare every pair
solutions.idea: For every pair take the gap d and its other-way-round version 1440 − d; keep the smallest.

solutions.title: Sort, then check neighbors and the wrap
solutions.idea: After sorting, only neighbors and the last-to-first pair across midnight can be closest.

solutions.title: 1440 buckets
solutions.idea: Mark each minute in a fixed array; a second mark means a duplicate. Walking the array visits the times in sorted order.

followups: Times now carry seconds too. What changes in the bucket version, and when does sorting win again?
Times arrive one at a time and you must report the current smallest gap after each. Which structure keeps that fast?
